intro: In this college you'll learn to describe the people you live with, talk about your street and neighbourhood, join local activities like the language café, compare places using Dutch comparatives, and politely complain about a noisy neighbour.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — your home and your street
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme eight. Its title is [[Huis, straat en buurt]], which means 'house, street and neighbourhood'. This is one of the most useful themes in the whole course, because in the Netherlands your neighbourhood is part of daily life. You greet people on the stairs, you chat by the front door, and you join activities close to home. So let's start with the key words. Your home is your [[huis]], the street you live on is your [[straat]], and the wider neighbourhood around you is the [[buurt]]. The people who live near you are your neighbours: a male neighbour is the [[buurman]], a female neighbour is the [[buurvrouw]], and together they are simply [[de buren]]. If you share a flat, the people you share it with are your [[huisgenoten]], your housemates. There is a lovely Dutch proverb about all this: [[Een goede buur is beter dan een verre vriend.]] It means 'a good neighbour is better than a faraway friend'. That idea runs through this whole theme. As always, I explain everything in English, but every Dutch phrase is spoken by a native voice, so repeat each one out loud after me. Ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Describing people: adjectives
paragraphs.text: To talk about housemates and neighbours, you need adjectives that describe people. A friendly, pleasant person is [[aardig]] or [[vriendelijk]]. The opposite, an annoying person, is [[vervelend]]. Someone calm and quiet is [[rustig]], while someone messy or noisy makes you say [[Hij maakt veel lawaai]], 'he makes a lot of noise'. A neat, tidy person is [[netjes]], and a helpful one is [[behulpzaam]]. So you might describe an ideal housemate like this: [[Mijn ideale huisgenoot is netjes, rustig en behulpzaam.]] That means 'my ideal housemate is tidy, calm and helpful'. To give your own opinion, use the verb [[vinden]], which means 'to find' or 'to think'. For example: [[Ik vind mijn buurvrouw heel aardig.]] To add a reason, use the little word [[omdat]], 'because' — and here is the trick: after [[omdat]] the verb jumps to the very end of the sentence. So you say [[Ik vind haar aardig, omdat zij mij vaak helpt.]] Notice how [[helpt]] sits right at the end. That word order feels strange at first, but with practice it becomes natural. Try describing your own neighbour out loud, using one adjective and one reason with [[omdat]].

paragraphs.heading: Comparing with the comparative
paragraphs.text: Now for some real grammar power: comparing two things. In Dutch you usually just add [[-er]] to an adjective. So [[groot]], meaning 'big', becomes [[groter]], 'bigger'. [[Rustig]] becomes [[rustiger]], 'quieter', and [[leuk]] becomes [[leuker]], 'nicer'. To say 'than', you use the word [[dan]]. For example: [[Mijn nieuwe buurt is rustiger dan de oude.]] That means 'my new neighbourhood is quieter than the old one'. Or, about your room: [[Mijn kamer is groter dan jouw kamer.]] Watch the spelling — [[groot]] has a double o, but [[groter]] keeps only one. A few words are irregular and you simply have to learn them. 'Good' is [[goed]], but 'better' is [[beter]]. 'Much' is [[veel]], but 'more' is [[meer]]. So you can say [[Deze straat is beter dan mijn vorige straat.]] There is also a neat way to say two things are equal: put the adjective between [[zo]] and [[als]]. For instance: [[Mijn straat is net zo gezellig als vroeger.]] The little word [[net]] stresses that they are exactly the same. With this pattern the adjective stays in its plain form, so it is [[zo groot als]], never the [[-er]] form.

paragraphs.heading: Your neighbourhood and the taalcafé
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about what is around you and what you can do nearby. A handy way to describe your area is [[er is]], 'there is', and [[er zijn]], 'there are'. So you might say [[Er is een mooi park naast mijn huis.]], 'there is a lovely park next to my house', or [[Er zijn veel activiteiten in de buurt.]], 'there are lots of activities in the neighbourhood'. To give your overall opinion, use [[Ik vind het hier fijn wonen.]], which means 'I like living here'. And to say you are content with something, use the very useful phrase [[tevreden zijn met]], 'to be satisfied with'. For example: [[Ik ben tevreden met mijn huisgenoten.]], 'I am happy with my housemates'. One activity I really recommend is the [[taalcafé]], a language café where you practise Dutch over coffee with other learners and friendly volunteers. You can say [[In het taalcafé oefen ik mijn Nederlands.]], 'at the language café I practise my Dutch'. Many neighbourhoods also hold a [[buurtfeest]], a street party where you meet everybody at once. Joining these is the fastest way to feel at home, because the people there are patient and warm. If someone asks [[Wat vind jij van de buurt?]], 'what do you think of the neighbourhood?', now you can answer with confidence.

paragraphs.heading: When you have a problem: last hebben van
paragraphs.text: Not every neighbour is easy, so let's learn how to handle a problem politely. The key expression is [[last hebben van]], which means 'to be bothered by' or 'to suffer from'. For example: [[Ik heb last van de buurman.]], 'I am bothered by the neighbour'. You can be specific: [[Ik heb last van het lawaai.]], 'the noise is bothering me'. A very common complaint is loud music at night, so you might explain [[Mijn buurman maakt 's avonds veel lawaai.]], 'my neighbour makes a lot of noise in the evening'. The Dutch way is to stay calm and talk to the person first, before going to the landlord, your [[verhuurder]]. A polite, gentle request works wonders: [[Kunt u alstublieft wat zachter doen?]], which means 'could you please be a bit quieter?'. Notice the polite [[u]] and the magic word [[alstublieft]], 'please'. You could also ask [[Wilt u de muziek na tien uur zachter zetten?]], 'would you turn the music down after ten o'clock?'. If you must, you can say [[Ik heb een probleem met mijn buurman, omdat hij rommel maakt.]], 'I have a problem with my neighbour, because he makes a mess'. Staying friendly almost always works better than complaining straight away.

paragraphs.heading: Putting it together — a doorstep chat
paragraphs.text: Let's put everything together in a real little scene. Imagine you have just moved in, and a neighbour says hello: [[Hoi! Jij bent net verhuisd, hè? Hoe bevalt de buurt?]], 'hi, you just moved in, right? How do you like the neighbourhood?'. You answer warmly: [[Heel goed, dank je. Ik vind het hier rustiger dan in mijn vorige straat.]], 'very good, thanks — I find it quieter here than in my previous street'. Then you mention a small worry: [[Alleen 's nachts hoor ik soms harde muziek. Ik heb een beetje last van de buurman.]], 'only at night I sometimes hear loud music; the neighbour bothers me a little'. Your new neighbour gives advice: [[Praat eerst rustig met hem.]], 'first talk calmly with him', and adds [[Dat is beter dan meteen klagen.]], 'that is better than complaining straight away'. Finally she invites you: [[Kom naar het buurtfeest, dan leer je iedereen kennen!]], 'come to the street party, then you'll get to know everyone'. And that is how a neighbourhood becomes a home. Practise this little conversation out loud with your partner today. You are doing wonderfully. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I'll see you in theme nine!
